articles.headline: INSTANTANEOUS ROUND-UP VIEWS.
articles.text:
INSTANTANEOUS ROUND-UP VIEWS.

We have remaining a few sets of Huffmann's instantaneous round-up views, representing the most interesting events of the range cattle industry. There are thirty-six well-executed photographs in the series, making an extremely interesting and realistic panorama of cowboy life. We will sell the complete set for $5 or,

THE COW BOY A YEAR AND THE SET, $6

This offer will probably be recalled soon, but the bargain can now be secured by calling on or addressing THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Display notice from the Cow Boy offering sets of Huffman's 36 instantaneous round-up photographs for $5, or $6 with a year's subscription.

articles.text: Every preparation is being made at St. Paul to have the coming ice carnival eclipse anything of the kind ever before attempted. A greatly improved ice palace will be built and taking last year's exhibition as a basis, everything will be done on an enlarged plan. Half-rates have been secured on all railroad lines leading into St. Paul.
articles.summary: St. Paul is preparing a larger ice carnival and ice palace, with half-rates on railroads into the city.

articles.text: There seems every probability of the opening of the Sioux Reservation at this session of Congress. The president is thought not to favor the plan very ardently but it is believed that enough votes can be secured to pass the bill over his veto. The people of the Black Hills are no better off than before the advent of the Fremont, Elkhorn & Missouri Valley R. R., in the matter of freight charges and are looking forward as eagerly as ever for relief in the way of active competition. The Manitoba, Northwestern and Milwaukee roads are casting longing eyes Hillswards and will build as soon as spring opens if the bill is passed.
articles.summary: The paper expects Congress to open the Sioux Reservation, possibly over the president's veto, and says several railroads would then build toward the Black Hills.

articles.text: At last the long agony is over and Judge Louis K. Church has been appointed governor of Dakota in place of our present governor Pierce, who persisted in his resignation after its acceptance had been refused by the president. Judge Church is recognized by all as an able man who will in all probabilty be satisfactorly to the people, except that it certainly seems time for a Dakota citizen to have the honor conferred upon him. Governor Pierce has been peculiarly fortunate and an exception to all previous governors of Dakota, no taint of corruption attaching to him. His administration has been so clean that even the jealous eyes of the disgruntted politicians of southern Dakota could see nothing to criticize.
articles.summary: Judge Louis K. Church has been appointed governor of Dakota in place of the resigning Governor Pierce, whose clean administration the paper praises.

articles.text: Telegrams from Huron indicate that the state (?) legislature in session there will disregard the restraining clause in their constitution and set the state government of South Dakota to running. The simple fact of the matter is, that had it not been for the insatiate greed for office that characterizes every one of the prime movers in the statehood movement, Dakota would long ago have been admitted to the Union. It is utterly impossibly for Congress to judge accurately of the sense of the people when represented by such self-elected mouth-pieces as the average Dakota politician. All in the world they want is office and to this alone is due the cry of division; two states making double the number of offices. We believe the majority of Dakota's citizens are in favor of admission and against division and admission. The only right way is to leave the matter to a popular vote.
articles.summary: Editorial attacking the South Dakota statehood legislature meeting at Huron and the division movement, urging a popular vote.

articles.text: There is nothing that will destroy a person's faith in mankind quicker than to become an editor. We heard positively and from authentic sources that Miss Lilly Roberts and Riley Brooks were married and as a consequence, published it as an item of news. In fact, there is no word of truth in the matter and we owe an especial apology to Miss Roberts for the unwelcome publicity given her. The Cow Boy has before been victimized in this same way and hereafter we will have to be present at the cermony or receive the assurance of the contracting parties to believe that the marriage has actually taken place.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy retracts its report that Miss Lilly Roberts and Riley Brooks had married and apologizes to Miss Roberts.

articles.text: Only 7,000 cattle arrived at the Chicago yards Monday and as a consequence prices ruled a little higher and sales were brisk. Sales of shipping cattle and feeders were slow, owing to the fact that many states have quarantined against Chicago. There were no northern rangers on the market, the season having practically closed for them two weeks ago.
articles.summary: Light Chicago receipts Monday lifted prices; quarantines slowed feeder sales and the northern range season closed two weeks ago.

articles.text: The Chicago live stock exchange and the National cattle growers' association of America, have each issued a series of resolutions condemnatory of the recent raise in rates adopted by the east-bound pool from Chicago. It appears that on the 1st. of last March the rates were raised $20 per car on live cattle, $43 per car on dressed beef, $40 per car on live sheep and $90 per car on dressed sheep. These resolutions are addressed to the live stock papers, to state legislatures and to Congress, in the hope that speedy legislation would relieve live stock interests from this additional incubus which is pressing the profit out of the business. No valid claim has yet been set up by the railroads that former rates were not profitable and the increase cannot but be regarded as exorbitant.
articles.summary: Cattlemen's organizations have condemned the east-bound railroad pool's freight-rate increases from Chicago.

articles.text: A law should be passed by the coming legislature, giving special protection to the beaver. This is an animal, harmless to the farmer and of great value to the owner of stock. It dams rivers, rendering them available for watering stock, when, if it were not for them, the cattle would have difficulty in getting enough to drink. The Heart river is dammed in several places by these interesting and industrious little animals and it is only from a spirit of wanton slaughter that they are killed. Unfortunately there are so many people in this country who never see a head without wanting to hit it, and they never see an animal that can move without wanting to shoot. Many beavers that would, if they had a chance, live lives of usefulness, have their careers cut short as a result of this slaughtering spirit. Will not the legislature come to their aid?—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Mandan Pioneer urging the legislature to protect beavers, whose dams on the Heart river help water stock.

articles.headline: Dakota Railroad Interest.
articles.text:
Despite the drought and poor crops Dakota seems to have considerable attraction for railroad men, and indications are at present that there will be considerable activity in railway building throughout the northwest in 1886. Marvin Hughitt, general manager of the Northwestern and President of the Omaha, called upon the president to-day and asked for an order allowing his road right of way through Fort Mead military reservation in the Black Hills. The power to grant this permission is vested in the President, but he firmly refused Mr. Hughitt's request. The latter retired from the White House very angry and asserted that he would go to Congress for the permission. This he promptly did, for within two hours after he left the White House Mr. Scott, of Pennsylvana, introduced in the House a bill to grant the desired right of way to the Fremont, Elkhorn and Misssouri Valley Road, under which name this branch of Mr. Hughitt's road masquerades.

J. J. Hill, of the Manitoba Road, is in the city, looking after his interests in the northwest, and to urge a bill which Delegate Toole, of Montana, to-day introduced granting the above road right of way throught the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation in Dakota and the Blackfeet Reservation in Montana. The new line is to start from Minot and cross the reservation on the line between townships 153 and 154, to follow the Missouri river by the most convenient route to the valley of the Milk river, through that valley to Fort Assinaboine, and thence southwesterly to the great falls of the Missouri. This will parallel the Northern Pacific to a considerable extent, as far as the accessible and valuable portions of Dakota and Montana are concerned.

Delegate Gifford offers a bill providing for the building of a bridge across the Missouri at or within five miles of Yankton, for the Yankton and Missoni Valley Railroad, and the extension of the Chicago and Northwestern Road.

Congressman Kieiner, of Indiana, also introduced a bill to allow the Duluth, Pierre and Black Hills R. R. to build a bridge across the Missouri at Pierre, Dak. This is an extension of the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul system, and the bridge will be constructed jointly by the Chicago and Northwestern and the above mentioned road, if authorized by Congress.—[The Inter Ocean.
articles.summary: Reprinted Washington dispatch (Inter Ocean) on railroad right-of-way and bridge bills affecting Dakota, including Hughitt's Fort Meade request and J. J. Hill's line from Minot across the Fort Berthold reservation.

articles.headline: Christmas at the Insane Asylum.
articles.text:
Desirous of making "Xmas" day at the asylum one of enjoyment and long to be pleasantly remembered by our unfortunate inmates, I again take the liberty of calling upon the many kind friends of the hospital, and ask them to contribute what they feel they can, either in money or suitable articles for the benefit and pleasure of our people on that day. If each individual will contribute only a very little, it will, in the aggregate, amount to a considerable sum with us, and be the means of affording real pleasure and benefit to our insane people. Without the kind and liberal assistance of friends in different parts of the territory we shall be unable to do for our patients this year what should be done in their behalf, and we trust that the benevolent ladies, who so generously aided and who did so much for our "Xmas" at the hospital last year, will not forget that many of the same sad hearts are with us still as well as a large number of new cases. Please let your gifts be general. We do not want much from any one. It is the little from the many that will make Christmas day at the asylum the pleasant oasis of the year and we will be most gratefully,

Your Obedient Servant,
O. W. Archibald, Supt.
articles.summary: Letter from asylum superintendent O. W. Archibald appealing for Christmas gifts for the territorial insane hospital's patients.

articles.headline: Horses and Drivers.
articles.text: Very many years ago I made up my mind that when there is a quarrel between a man and a horse, in nine cases out of ten the man is in the wrong. Continued observation has only served to confirm this belief. The radical error into which drivers fall is the belief that the horse knows perfectly what is wanted of him, and will do it. Then the driver proceeds to show that he is the master, and in the vast majority of cases the horse has not the slightest idea why he is so treated. For a horse to understand instantly what his driver desires, there must exist a pleasant feeling between them. The horse must feel a confidence in his driver. With one driver a horse will show himself fearless of locomotives, and with another he will dread them. One man will drive a horse fifton miles with no more fatigue to the animal than another driver will produce by driving him only ten. Nothing tends more to cruelty to animals than cowardice. The man who has a lurking fear of his beast is the man who treats him the more harshly. The man who is afraid of no horse, is just the man who treats him kindly. He is perfectly aware that there is always danger with horses; but he also knows that this does not depend upon the horse, but mostly comes from some extraneous sources, the bad driving of others whom he meets on the road, or accident of some sort. He has a friendly feeling toward his beast, as being a willing and useful servant and companion, ready to do his whole duty. So there springs up a pleasant feeling on both sides, the horse is encouraged and cheerful, and gets through with his work easily and well. Such a driver gets vastly more from his horses than does the cruel one. They come in fresh and they feed and sleep well, and begin the next day's work under favorable conditions. Age tells but slowly on them, at 15 and 16 years such horses still show speed and endurance, and are still gay and free-goers, with years of usefulness before them, whereas the cruel man's horse is used up long before this time. There should be kindness simply from kind feeling, but it does not the less certainly bring its material reward.—[Humane Record.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Humane Record arguing that kind drivers get more from their horses than cruel ones.

articles.text: George Myers returned Sunday night with Fred Willard. A warrant had been sworn out for his arrest by the Montana Stockgrower's Association for shipping two steers claimed not to belong to him, in a car of Maltese Cross steers. The whole matter bears the ear-marks of a put up job as the facts in the case are perfectly plain: George has for several years been working at the Maltese Cross ranch and has constantly put his wages into horses and cattle. Some time ago he bought a few head and before they were all branded, two of them escaped. Soon after, these two were found near Garner creek on the Maltese Cross range and in the presence of witnesses, one of whom was Sylvanus Ferris, a part owner of the range, were branded with Myers' brand. When the Maltese Cross outfit shipped their cattle this fall, George put in the two head spoken of and sold them in Chicago. He then went to his home near Wooster, Ohio and would have returned voluntarily this week or next to resume his old position on the Maltese Cross ranch, but was arrested and brought back as narrated. The warrant for his arrest was made out by the Montana Stockgrowers' Association, claiming that the cattle belonged to the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association. This quashes the suit on its face, as a by-law of the Little Misouri River Association states distinctly that mavericks, and only mavericks under any circumstances could belong to the association, should be branded with the brand on which the maverick is found. One of the managers of the Maltese Cross outfit, on whose range the animals were found, not only knew the cattle, but himself assisted George in branding them. The case in a nut-shell is this. Mr. Ferris could have claimed the cattle but knowing they belonged to George, turned them over to him. It is a matter that in no way affects anyone except the owners of the Maltese Cross range. As these gentlemen happen to be Theodore Roosevelt and Messrs, Ferris & Merrifield, and as they all claim that George owned the cattle, "the wayfaring man though a fool" can see that George is not guilty. To George's friends, the charge is nothing if not foolish. That he should tarnish a reputation gained by years of honest, faithful work for the sake of two head of cattle, is a thought that cannot be entertained for a moment. He is now bound over in $1,000 bonds to the circuit court, having waived examination. Ferris & Merrifield and Mm. Dantz are his sureties and if necessary every name on the river could be added to the list. We will prophesy right here that the case will never come to a trial as no grand jury on earth can find sufficient evidence in the case to bring it to trial.
articles.summary: George Myers, a longtime Maltese Cross hand, was brought back from Ohio on a Montana Stockgrowers' Association warrant for shipping two steers; the paper defends him, noting the range's owners, Theodore Roosevelt and Ferris & Merrifield, all say the cattle were his. ("Mm. Dantz" as printed; probably Wm. Dantz.)
